title: COMPACT: Composite Visual Teaching
one_liner: Instead of randomly picking training images and questions, pick fewer images but write questions that layer multiple skills together, so each example teaches more.
lead: Multimodal models (machines that read images and answer questions about them) are usually trained on huge datasets. COMPACT finds a smarter way: use far fewer training images, but write multi-layered questions for each one that demand multiple visual skills at once. The model learns faster from fewer examples because each complex question creates a bigger, more informative learning gap than a simple one.

problem.h2: The waste in random data collection
paras: Today's multimodal models learn by reading thousands of images paired with text questions. But most of these pairs are simple: 'What color is this?' or 'Is there a dog?' The model learns quickly from the first few thousand, then learns slower from the rest. Yet datasets keep growing to a million examples because nobody knows which ones actually matter.

A beginner might try: 'Pick only the examples where the model guesses wrong.' But that is expensive — you have to train the model, see where it fails, then collect new data. You end up training many times.

callout.html: Most training images are paired with questions so simple they teach little. You waste data budget.

steps.text: Pick an image from the full dataset.
List basic visual tasks in this image: object detection, counting, scene understanding, spatial reasoning, color naming.
Write ONE multi-part question that asks for multiple of these skills at once, e.g., 'How many red cars are parked to the left of the building?'
Use a language model to generate a detailed, accurate answer combining all those skills.
Use this composite example instead of ten simple ones, so dataset size drops 10x but learning per example jumps.

paras: COMPACT does not change which images you use. It changes the questions paired with each image — from simple, single-skill questions to complex, multi-skill ones.

hidden.name: how many basic skills a question bundles
paras: The paper's key insight is that not all questions are equally valuable. A simple question like 'What color?' teaches only one skill. A composite question like 'What are the colors of all vehicles on the left side of the image?' bundles object recognition, spatial reasoning, and color understanding in one example.

COMPACT measures this by identifying atomic visual capabilities (recognize objects, count instances, understand spatial layout, describe relationships, infer properties) and tracking how many of these a synthesized question demands. Questions that require three or four skills are worth more than ten questions each asking one skill.

heat.caption: Darker means the question demands more composite skills. Marked questions taught COMPACT's model better.

reads.html: A good training question is not just accurate — it forces the model to use many visual skills at once, like a dance that practices multiple moves in one routine.

The paper operationalizes skill compositionality by synthesizing questions that combine atomic visual capabilities, then measures performance gains when training data is filtered to high-compositionality examples.

mechanism.h2: Why layering skills together teaches faster
paras: A model learns by comparing its guess to the right answer and adjusting itself to close the gap. If the gap is small (a simple question the model almost gets right), the adjustment is tiny and slow, because the model is already close and has little to learn. If the gap is large and informative (a complex question that forces the model to strengthen multiple skills), the adjustment is bigger and better-aimed, because the model must move in multiple directions at once — object detection one way, spatial reasoning another, counting a third — all tied to the same answer.

COMPACT's mechanism: when you combine multiple skills in one question, you create a larger, more informative learning gap. The model cannot guess right by half-remembering just one skill — it must activate and tune object detection, spatial reasoning, counting, and color understanding together. That forces a big, coherent adjustment that sculpts interconnected structure faster, because all those skills reinforce each other in a single problem — the model tightens them together instead of learning each one in isolation over ten separate examples. So ten examples with composite questions teach the model more than one hundred simple ones.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Baseline: 100 training examples, each asking one simple skill (color naming or object detection).
COMPACT: 10 examples. Question 1 asks 'count objects AND describe colors' (2 skills). Question 2 asks 'objects AND layout AND relationships' (3 skills).
Average skills per COMPACT question: 2.5. If each skill reduces data needed by 40%, then 10 × (1 + 0.4 + 0.4 + 0.4 + 0.4) ≈ 30 effective example-units.

Result: 10 COMPACT examples teach as much as ~30 simple ones, so you can reach 100-example performance with 30-33 total examples, a 67% reduction. Real COMPACT achieves 90% reduction, meaning skills are higher-weight and/or synthesis is very precise.

math.note: The more skills a question bundles, the fewer total examples the model needs to learn all of them.

items.html: If a language model writes a composite answer that contradicts the image, the model learns the wrong thing. Solution: use a strong base model to synthesize answers, and optionally have a human spot-check a sample.

items.b: Composing skills that do not cohere.
items.html: If you force a question to ask for, say, object detection and sentiment analysis (which requires text in the image), you create an unnatural, ambiguous example. Solution: identify which atomic skills naturally co-occur in an image before composing them.

If a model is already weak, jumping straight to complex composite questions can overwhelm it. It needs some easy examples to build basic skills first. Solution: gradually increase compositionality during training, or mix 80% composite with 20% simple.

Careful skill selection, accurate synthetic answers, and gradual compositionality ramp make COMPACT work well. When measured in real training runs (not theory), the paper shows 90% data reduction while holding performance steady.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small visual instruction tuning setup: take a 10-class image dataset (e.g., CIFAR-10 scaled to higher resolution, or a simple image classification benchmark), and split it into two training pipelines.

Pipeline A (naive): randomly sample 1000 image-question pairs, each asking one simple skill ('What color is the main object?' or 'Is there a vehicle?'). Train a small multimodal model (e.g., CLIP-based) for a fixed number of steps. Measure accuracy on a held-out test set of complex questions that mix multiple skills.

Pipeline B (COMPACT): sample only 100 images, but synthesize 10 composite questions per image by hand or using a small language model (e.g., asking 'Count all red objects on the left of the image'). Train the same model for the same number of steps. Measure accuracy on the same complex test set.
The demo succeeds if Pipeline B (100 images, 1000 examples total, all composite) reaches at least 90% of Pipeline A's accuracy (1000 simple examples), proving that compositionality compresses data.
demo.closing: If COMPACT data hits 100%+ of baseline accuracy with 10x fewer images, compositionality is the lever — questions that demand multiple skills teach faster because each one forces the model to align and tighten many skill-pathways in one coherent adjustment.
